Focal effect: -0.1777 g of day-14 mass per additional sibling in the rearing brood; SE 0.0174; t = -10.20; residual df 2547; p < 0.001; rearing-nest random-intercept variance 0.63 (SD 0.79 g). Sensitivity check: refitting without the sex covariate (n = 3,635, all 440 rearing broods, df 3630) gives -0.1812 g (SE 0.0157, t = -11.58), confirming robustness. Limitation: crossed hatch-nest random effect not fit (statsmodels), so genetic-origin clustering is absorbed only via year and randomization; the rearing nest (competition environment) is the primary modeled cluster. Effect = -0.15364 g (SE 0.01185, z = -12.964, p = 2.0e-38 normal-reference; t with df=396 gives p=9.1e-33 as sensitivity), n=3315 chicks (excluded only chicks missing day-14 mass, manipulation value, or realized brood size; of 3720 rows), 397 rearing-nest clusters. Missing-value policy: sex unknowns (n≈1082) kept as their own factor level; rear_nest_OH complete. This realized-competition operationalization is consistent with prior fits under other operationalizations (manipulated per-chick effect -0.180 g, SE 0.016; enlarged-vs-reduced contrast -1.07 g, SE 0.092), so the conclusion is robust: sibling competition reduces nestling growth. rows.note: Focal analysis: rearing-brood-level OLS of brood-mean size-corrected day-14 mass on the brood-size manipulation. Outcome: for each chick with complete day-14 weight and tarsus, size-corrected mass = residuals of OLS of day_14_weight on day_14_tarsus_length (pooled slope 1.042 g/mm, R2=0.358); these residuals were averaged within rearing brood (rear_nest_breed_ID x hatch_year). Focal predictor: net_rearing_manipulation (net chicks added to the rearing nest, signed: positive = experimentally enlarged, negative = reduced, 0 = unmanipulated), entered as a single continuous term; its coefficient is the change in brood-mean size-corrected mass (g) per net extra sibling. Covariates: year factor and rearing-nest hatch date (rear_nest_OH); chick sex drops out at brood level. Exclusions: only rearing broods lacking complete mass/tarsus or rear-nest hatch date information; 440 broods covering 3,635 measured chicks contributed. Observation unit: rearing brood (independent clusters, so OLS with conventional SEs; within-brood chick dependence handled by aggregation). Results: estimate -0.1138 g (SE 0.0131), t = -8.689, df = 435, p = 7.5e-17, n = 440 broods, R2 = 0.186. Robustness: chick-level mixed models (tarsus: -0.065 mm, SE 0.008; PC1 index: -0.173 SD, SE 0.016; condition: -0.109 g, SE 0.0145) and a GEE exchangeable clustered on rearing nest (-0.108 g, robust SE 0.0136) give the same substantive conclusion: each experimentally added sibling reduces nestling growth, here by about 0.11 g of size-corrected day-14 mass per extra chick.
rows.predictor: net_rearing_manipulation: net number of chicks added to (positive) or removed from (negative) the rearing nest, 0 for unmanipulated; effect reported as change in brood-mean size-corrected day-14 mass (g) per one net extra sibling

rows.note: Brood-size manipulation experiment (cross-fostered enlargements/reductions plus unmanipulated broods), Wytham Wood 2001-2003. Focal model: OLS linear regression day_14_tarsus_length ~ net_rearing_manipulation + factor(hatch_year) + factor(chick_sex_molec) + rear_nest_CS, with uncertainty from a cluster bootstrap: 1,000 resamples of rearing nests within year (clusters resampled with replacement, year composition preserved), SE = SD of resampled manipulation coefficients, t = estimate/SE with cluster-based df = 316 clusters - 1 = 315. Complete-case exclusions: 1,182 of 3,720 chicks dropped for missing values (predominantly unknown molecular sex); day-14 tarsus and the manipulation variable are complete. Focal effect: -0.0621 mm day-14 tarsus per additional sibling (cluster-bootstrap SE 0.0084, t = -7.42, df = 315, percentile bootstrap CI [-0.080, -0.046], p < 0.001). Larger manipulation values mean more siblings hence more competition (as_declared); the negative sign indicates each additional sibling reduces nestling day-14 tarsus growth by ~0.06 mm. Because the manipulation was experimentally randomized within hatching-date/brood-size-matched pairs, the coefficient is a causal estimate of the sibling-competition effect; post-manipulation brood size (the mediator) was deliberately not adjusted for, and rear-nest clutch size predates the manipulation so it cannot block the causal path. Cross-checks (other scales/structures, not converted): GEE exchangeable-robust on tarsus gave -0.0660 mm (SE 0.0083, t = -7.98); mass-scale models (GEE, mixed model, cluster-robust OLS) gave -0.170 to -0.180 g per additional sibling (t = -10.2 to -11.6). Observation unit: individual chick alive and measured at day 14. The conclusion is stable across outcome measure and inference method.
rows.predictor: net_rearing_manipulation: continuous signed net number of chicks added to the rearing nest (positive = brood enlarged, negative = reduced, 0 = unmanipulated); effect reported in millimeters of day-14 tarsus length per additional sibling

rows.note: Outcome: day_14_tarsus_length (mm), complete in file. Exposure: binary experimental contrast between rearing nests — enlarged (net_rearing_manipulation > 0, indicator = 1) vs reduced (net_rearing_manipulation < 0, indicator = 0); unmanipulated broods (net = 0) excluded because they were not matched to the manipulated pairs. Covariates: hatch_year factor (2001–2003), chick molecular sex factor (unknown sex "." excluded), rearing-nest hatch date (rear_nest_OH). Estimator: OLS with two-way cluster-robust sandwich SEs (small-sample corrected), clustered jointly on rearing nest within year (251 clusters) and hatch nest within year (277 clusters), handling dependence among chicks sharing either natal or rearing nests without random-effect assumptions. Focal estimate = coefficient on the enlarged-vs-reduced contrast: −0.374 mm difference in day-14 tarsus (enlarged broods produce lighter-skeletoned chicks); SE 0.043; t = −8.71, t-type inference, df = 2081; p ≈ 4.3e-16. Fitted n = 2,087 chicks (1,311 enlarged, 776 reduced); observation unit = chick. Robustness: a cross-classified mixed model (rear-nest random intercept + hatch-nest variance component, REML) gave −0.385 mm (SE 0.049), and a continuous per-extra-sibling manipulation slope gave −0.065 mm/sibling (SE 0.008) — all consistent in sign and magnitude. No outcome values were imputed; exclusions were only rows missing net manipulation, tarsus, molecular sex, or rearing-nest hatch date.

rows.note: Focal analysis: two-stage least-squares instrumental-variable regression of day-14 nestling mass on realized rearing-brood size at the start of rearing (rear_Cs_at_start_of_rearing, 2-18 nest-mates), instrumented by the randomized net_rearing_manipulation. Both stages adjust for factor(hatch_year), factor(chick_sex_molec), and rear_nest_OH; standard errors are cluster-robust by rearing nest within year (292 clusters). First stage is strong: manipulation coefficient 0.957 chicks per chick manipulated, t = 21.83, R2 = 0.69. Focal 2SLS estimate: -0.1739 g of day-14 mass per exogenously induced additional nest-mate (cluster-robust SE 0.0170, t = -10.22, df = 287, p < 0.001, n = 2,367 chicks in 292 broods; 1,353 of 3,720 chicks excluded as missing covariates, predominantly molecular sex). Observation unit: individual chick; test statistic: t. Causal interpretation: local average treatment effect of an exogenously imposed extra sibling on nestling growth, identified by the randomized cross-fostering manipulation under the exclusion restriction (manipulation affects growth only via nest-mate number) and within-pair randomization; near-perfect compliance (first-stage slope ~0.96) means the LATE approximates the average brood-size effect in this population. Cross-checks: direct GEE on net_rearing_manipulation gave -0.1777 g (SE 0.0169, t = -10.53); REML mixed model -0.1777 g (SE 0.0174); cluster-robust OLS on manipulation -0.1699 g (SE 0.0165); naive OLS on realized brood size -0.1502 g (SE 0.0140) on the same IV sample, with the IV estimate more negative as expected since natural brood-size variation dilutes the observational association. Conclusion: sibling competition causally reduces nestling growth by ~0.17 g per additional sibling.

rows.note: Brood-size manipulation experiment, Wytham Wood 2001–2003. Focal model: REML linear mixed model day_14_weight ~ factor(rearing-brood treatment: enlarged/reduced/unmanipulated, decoded via rear_nest_trt 5/6/7 cross-referenced with net_rearing_manipulation; reduced as reference) + factor(hatch_year) + rear_nest_CS, with a random intercept for rearing nest within year (435 clusters). Complete-case exclusions: 126 of 3,720 chicks dropped for missing values; no chick missing day-14 mass or treatment. Focal contrast (enlarged vs reduced): -1.0723 g (SE 0.0936, t = -11.46, df 3588, p < 0.001). Because enlarged and reduced broods were cross-foster matched on hatching date and original brood size, differing only in the manipulation, this contrast is a causal estimate of the sibling-competition effect: chicks reared with more siblings are over 1 g lighter at day 14. Unmanipulated broods fall between the two treatments (-0.23 g vs reduced), consistent with a monotone competition dose. Orientation as_declared: the contrast is coded 1 = enlarged (more competition) vs 0 = reduced; the negative sign indicates more competition reduces nestling growth. Continuous-dose cross-checks corroborate the finding (-0.07 to -0.18 g per additional sibling depending on adjustment set and exposure operationalization).

Unmanipulated broods (trt 7) retained as a non-focal third level to help estimate background effects

rows.note: Focal estimate: effect of the experimentally manipulated number of siblings (net_rearing_manipulation, signed net chicks added: positive = enlarged brood, negative = reduced, 0 = unmanipulated) on nestling growth, operationalized as size-corrected day-14 mass (residuals of day_14_weight regressed linearly on day_14_tarsus_length within the fitted sample; weight~tarsus slope 1.020, R2 0.349). Exclusions: only rows missing day-14 weight, day-14 tarsus, net_rearing_manipulation, or rear_nest_OH were dropped; chicks with unknown molecular sex were RETAINED as an explicit 'unknown' sex level (n=1,082), giving n=3,635 chicks in 440 rear nests and 484 hatch nests. Focal result: estimate = -0.1137 g size-corrected mass per net extra sibling, SE = 0.0128, t = -8.85, p = 8.8e-19; inferential df (residual) = 3,628; observation unit = chick. Random variances: rear-nest 0.370, hatch-nest 0.112, residual 0.324. Result is consistent with sensitivity fits using day-14 tarsus (-0.065 mm/chick, SE 0.008) and a PC1 size index (-0.173 SD/chick, SE 0.016), and with a complete-sex complete-case fit (-0.109 g, SE 0.014), so the negative sibling-competition effect is robust. The manipulation was experimentally assigned (cross-fostered broods matched for hatch date and size), so the coefficient is interpretable causally as the effect of sibling competition on nestling growth.

rows.note: Final verified focal analysis. Blue tit nestling growth vs sibling competition, Wytham Wood 2001-2003, all 3,720 chicks alive and measured at day 14 (available-case/missing-indicator rule: molecular sex unknown for 1,094 chicks enters as its own category; zero exclusions). Focal model: Gaussian GEE, exchangeable working correlation across chicks within rearing nest within year (453 clusters, within-brood correlation 0.606); mean model day_14_weight ~ d14_rear_nest_brood_size + factor(hatch_year) + sex(1/2/unknown) + rear_nest_OH; empirical robust sandwich SE; large-sample Wald z inference (df not applicable, asymptotic in 453 clusters). Native effect: -0.08347 g of day-14 mass per additional nestling in the rearing brood (robust SE 0.01310, z = -6.373, p < 0.001). Interpretation: each additional competing sibling reduces nestling day-14 mass by ~0.08 g; more siblings = more competition = less growth, hence as_declared with negative sign. Verified by an independent reproducibility script re-fitting from raw data.csv with identical results. Caveats: realized day-14 brood size is partly post-manipulation, so this is a conditional phenotypic association; the randomized manipulation itself gives a corroborating causal estimate of ~-0.17 g per extra chick. Robust across REML mixed model, cluster-robust OLS, and GEE, both exposure constructions (manipulation and realized brood size), and both missing-data rules (complete-case and missing-category).
